name: Scent layering (body wash, lotion, fragrance)

lead: Scent layering uses products from the same scent family, such as body wash, lotion and fragrance, so the smell builds, lasts longer and feels coherent.

The fragrance industry promotes a version of it: scented bath oil, shower gel or lotion in the morning, a lighter eau de toilette in the afternoon, and perfume at pulse points in the evening. General references say hydrated skin holds fragrance longer. No published trials of layering were found.

paras: People pick matching or complementary products, apply wash and lotion after showering, then add fragrance on top, and refresh through the day.
Fragrance ingredients can be allergenic, and more scented products means more potential exposure. No layering-specific studies were found.

angle.text: Users stack matching body wash, lotion and fragrance so their scent builds in layers and lasts longer through the day. The fragrance industry promotes versions of the practice.

lead: Scent layering is the practice of using matching or complementary scented products, such as body wash, lotion, deodorant and fragrance, in sequence so that the smell builds, lasts longer and reads as a single signature. People use it to smell consistently good through a whole day, which looksmaxxing communities treat as part of overall presentation, grooming and attractiveness.[1]

The fragrance industry promotes a version of the technique: scented bath oil, shower gel or lotion in the morning, a lighter eau de toilette in the afternoon, and perfume at pulse points in the evening.[2] Enthusiasts go further in two directions. Some buy a whole product line built around one scent, while others blend several fragrances or fragrance oils on the skin; one looksmax.org user asked how to reproduce results that a forum guide author attributed to blending popular designer scents.[3]

Reference sources say wear time depends on concentration, with cologne lasting around 2 hours, eau de toilette 2 to 4 and perfume 6 to 8 hours or more, and that drier skin holds fragrance for less time than skin with more oil.[2] That is the rationale proponents give for pairing a scent with a moisturising lotion. No published trial has tested layering itself, and research on fragrance mostly concerns allergy and ingredient safety rather than how people smell to others.[4]

paras: Layering means building a scent in steps. A scented wash leaves a faint base on the skin, a lotion from the same line seals it in, and a fragrance in the same family sits on top. Industry guidance describes a lighter scent early in the day and a heavier one later as another form of layering.[2]

Wikipedia lists approximate aromatic-compound levels of 15 to 30 percent for parfum, 15 to 20 percent for eau de parfum, 5 to 15 percent for eau de toilette and 2 to 3 percent for eau de cologne, and notes that the labels are imprecise because houses use different dilutions, so an eau de toilette from one brand can be stronger than an eau de parfum from another.[2] Layering is often described as a way to extend the shorter-lasting, lighter concentrations.

Perfumers describe a fragrance as a pyramid. Top notes such as citrus, mint and lavender are light molecules that evaporate first and shape the first impression; heart notes such as jasmine or sandalwood form the body as those fade; base notes such as amber, tobacco and musk become noticeable about half an hour after application and add depth.[2] Layering by matching the same note family across wash, lotion and fragrance is meant to reinforce the base so the heart and base persist.[2]

Traditional guidance for pure perfume is to apply it to pulse points such as the wrists, neck, behind the ears and inner elbows, where body warmth is said to release the scent.[2] Layered products are applied to the whole body in the shower or after it, while fragrance goes on selected points.

The same reference says dry skin does not hold fragrance as long as skin with more oil, that hydration can affect how long a scent lasts, and that diet, such as spicy or fatty food, and some medications can change how a scent smells on a given wearer.[2] Proponents use these points to explain why a lotion is part of the routine and why the same fragrance can smell different from person to person.

Many brands sell wash, lotion, deodorant and fragrance under one scent name so that customers can layer. Behind the brands, a small number of fragrance houses compose scents for personal-care products; a 2017 Hacker News thread discussing a report that scents in several body washes came from the supplier Givaudan named other large suppliers such as Symrise, Firmenich, IFF and Takasago.[5] In the same thread one commenter said unscented body washes are less common in shops because many buyers want to smell clean, not only be clean.[5]

Fragrance is a regular topic on looksmax.org, where users ask for recommendations, trade favourite colognes and discuss which scents suit parties, dates or daily wear. Thread titles include general recommendation requests, a fragrance megaguide, an introduction to inexpensive fragrance clones and a discussion of how much a scent can add to overall attractiveness.[1][6][7][8]

Blending is also discussed: one thread asks how to replicate a layered fragrance approach described in a facial-improvement guide, listing designer scents and replica oils the poster owns.[3] Skin and body-wash choices appear in separate skincare threads, where users ask which wash and moisturiser to use.[9]

Natural and synthetic perfume materials include compounds that can cause allergic reactions, and a long history of use does not by itself establish safety.[2] Wikipedia notes that some fragrances can trigger asthma, headaches and skin reactions, and that balsam of Peru is used as a marker for perfume allergy in patch testing.[2] Under an EU directive, 26 recognised fragrance allergens have had to be listed on labels since March 2005, with thresholds of 0.001 percent for leave-on and 0.01 percent for rinse-off products.[2]

Contact dermatitis is described as the most common reaction to fragrance. One estimate cited on Wikipedia is that 1.7 to 4.1 percent of the general population has contact allergy to a common fragrance mix, and that products labelled fragrance-free can still contain lesser-known fragrance chemicals.[4] Stacking several scented products raises the number of fragrance ingredients in contact with skin.

Scent layering sits alongside deodorant and antiperspirant use, moisturising, choosing fragrance by season or occasion, and decanting or sampling fragrances before committing to a bottle. It is a grooming habit rather than a product, so its cost depends on whether people use a single brand line or mix budget and luxury items.
No studies found. Related research concerns fragrance allergy and patch testing,[4] and no published trial has tested layered or blended fragrances for how attractive wearers are judged to be.

lore.intro: Layering is discussed as a way to make a scent last and read as deliberate, often alongside fragrance recommendations and blending experiments.[1][3]

timeline.event: Aqua Admirabilis, a forerunner of eau de cologne, is created, according to Wikipedia's history of perfume.[2]
Guerlain's Jicky becomes the first fragrance labelled a parfum with a high concentration, per Wikipedia.[2]
Eau de parfum and parfum de toilette gain popularity, creating more concentration tiers to layer between.[2]
Michael Edwards creates the Fragrance Wheel, a classification of scent families.[2]
EU mandatory labelling of 26 fragrance allergens takes effect on 11 March.[2]
A Hacker News discussion of a report on Givaudan scents in body wash draws 23 comments.[5]
